Game for me to learn and kids to play
Fireworks fun
2d platform view horizontal
Browser based
JavaScript
Advanced graphics like WebGL to allow dynamic effects

Gameplay
Press a key
Firework launches
Any key will launch 1
Keys can be chorded
Sequential Combos
Key press sets random seed which changes effects, colours, patterns
Chords and combos launch multiples
Sound effects follow sprites
Dynamic music following pace and quantity

Hypothesis
Random but predictable
Patterns will emerge and be learned by player
Like playing a piano player can come up with combos and chords to create " visual music"

## Claude responded: Here's how I'd break this down.
Brainstorming concept ideas without building anything yet.Brainstorming concept ideas without building anything yet.Here's how I'd break this down.
**What's solid**

• One-key-launches-one-firework is a great core loop — instant feedback, zero learning curve for kids.
• Chords and combos add depth without adding buttons. That's the right move for a game two very different age groups will play.
• "Random but predictable" is the key design idea. Seed the randomness off the key itself (not just Math.random()), so pressing "J" tends to feel like "J" every time, but never identical. That's what lets patterns get learned.

**Open questions worth deciding before I build**

• **Combo detection** — do you want:

• *Chords*: keys held within a short window (e.g. 80ms) launch together
• *Sequences*: a pattern typed in order (like a fighting-game combo) unlocks a special effect
• Or both? Both is more interesting but harder to teach the player. Might need a small on-screen hint system so kids discover combos instead of needing a manual.

• **What does a combo actually change?** Options: more rockets, a shape (heart, spiral, ring, willow), a color family, or a sound/music shift. Probably some mix, tied to what the keys "mean" — e.g. WASD does something different from number keys.
• **Seeding**: keycode alone repeats the same firework forever, which gets boring. Keycode + press count + rough timing gives you "family resemblance" (predictable) with variation (random) — that matches your hypothesis better.
• **Sound**: two options — synthesize everything live with the Web Audio API (whoosh + crackle + boom, no files, totally self-contained), or use a few short baked-in audio samples for richer sound. Synthesis is more "impressive tech" and zero load time; samples sound better faster. I'd lean synthesis since it fits the "advanced graphics/effects" spirit and keeps the file self-contained.
• **Dynamic music**: tie tempo/density to *rate of key presses* over the last few seconds, not total fireworks. A player mashing keys gets a frantic, busy score; a player who pauses gets it settle back down. Simple to build with a scheduler and a few oscillators.
• **Visual style**: WebGL for the particles (additive blending gives that glowing trail look for free). I'd keep the ground/skyline simple — dark gradient sky, a silhouette horizon — so the fireworks stay the whole show.
• **Since it's partly for you to learn**: I'll comment the code to explain the WebGL/particle/audio patterns as we go, not just ship a black box.

Want me to lock in some of these (chords vs sequences vs both, synth vs sample audio) before I start building, or should I just make the calls and you can redirect once you see it running?

Both chords and sequences.
I want to separate the layers too.
AudioVisual layer takes action input, decides how to present.
Action layer takes control input, decides the spec of each firework.
Control layer takes input from player, send to action layer.
Player can be same device or remote. Eg web sockets across two devices, players see same things, play together. Keep remote layer out of scope for now. Just want enough abstraction to allow easy swaps of presentation layer and player inputs.

I'm thinking very MVC because that's my webapp Dev experience. But I've not done game before. Does this make sense?

Keep this discussions about design only no code yet

## Claude responded: Yes, it makes sense — and the three-layer split is the right call.
Outlining a spec contract and naming feedback for the layers.Outlining a spec contract and naming feedback for the layers.Yes, it makes sense — and the three-layer split is the right call. A few thoughts on shaping it well.
**The MVC instinct is right, but it's not quite MVC**
Web apps run on request/response: a click happens, you handle it, you're done until the next click. A game runs on a loop — something needs to keep updating positions and redrawing even when nobody's pressing a key (particles falling, trails fading). So the model here is closer to what game engines call **input → simulation → render**, not classic MVC. Same idea as yours, different shape underneath. Worth knowing so you're not surprised when "no request in flight" doesn't apply here.
**What each layer should own**

• **Control**: only knows about raw input. Key down, key up, how long a key was held. It should *not* know what a chord or sequence is — its job is just to turn "player pressed J at this moment" into a clean, normalized event and hand it off. This is what makes swapping in a remote player later painless: as long as a remote input arrives in the same shape (who pressed what, when), Action never has to know the difference.
• **Action**: this is where the rules live. Chord windows, sequence matching, and turning "what got pressed" into "what firework should happen" — position, pattern, color family, size, how many. It owns the game's memory: recent key history, per-key seed state. Nothing about canvas or sound belongs here.
• **AudioVisual**: takes what Action decided and makes it look and sound like something. Owns the particle positions, the WebGL draw calls, the oscillators. It shouldn't need to know *why* a firework happened, only *what* it should look and sound like.

**The thing that actually makes swapping easy**
The layer names matter less than the shape of the data passed between them. What you really want to define is a small, stable "firework spec" — the object Action hands to AudioVisual. Something like: where it launches from, what pattern, what color seed, how big, how it was triggered (single key, chord, sequence). If that shape stays stable, you can rewrite the renderer entirely, or swap keyboard for a websocket feed, without touching the middle layer. That contract is worth thinking through on paper before any code — it's doing more of the work than the layer boundaries themselves.
**One thing to decide now for the multiplayer seam**
You said remote is out of scope, but one decision now saves a rewrite later: when two players eventually share a screen, do they see the *same* firework, or does each device just render its own copy? If it's the same firework, the seed has to be decided once — in Action, at the moment the spec is created — and that finished spec gets sent to every device, never recomputed locally. If Action instead just says "key J was pressed" and lets AudioVisual pick the seed, two devices would draw two different fireworks for the same keystroke. Doesn't need building now, just means: Action always finishes the spec before handing it off, never leaves randomness for the presentation layer to decide.
**Small thing that's easy to miss coming from web dev**
Chords and sequences both depend on *time*, not frames — "these keys landed within 80ms of each other," "this sequence timed out after 2 seconds." Use real timestamps for that logic, not a frame counter, since frame rate will vary across devices and you don't want combo detection to depend on how fast someone's browser is drawing.
Want to sketch the firework spec's fields next, or talk through how Action should track chord/sequence state?
